title: DST Placement Coordination
name: DST Placement Coordination
metaTitle: DST Placement Coordination in San Jose, CA
metaDescription: DST placement coordination for San Jose 1031 exchangers stepping back from active management of long-held industrial and flex property.

sections.html: A Delaware Statutory Trust placement gives a San Jose exchanger a way to complete a 1031 into a fractional, professionally managed interest instead of taking on another building to run directly. We coordinate this option most often for long-time owner-operators along the Monterey Road corridor or in Edenvale who are ready to step back from active management without giving up the tax deferral. It's a decision we walk through carefully, since it changes the owner's relationship to the asset in ways that go well beyond the tax mechanics.

sections.heading: Who Actually Uses a DST Placement Here
sections.html: The owners who come to us about DST placements tend to share a profile: they've run an industrial or flex building in San Jose for fifteen, twenty, thirty years, they're tired of tenant calls and roof repairs, and they want the exchange to actually reduce their workload rather than trade one management headache for another. A DST interest lets that capital keep working under the exchange rules while someone else runs the day-to-day.

sections.heading: How a DST Fits Inside the Exchange Timeline
sections.html: A DST interest can be identified on the 45-day letter and closed within the 180-day window exactly like a directly owned replacement property, and it can also serve as the fallback candidate on an identification list when a directly owned replacement falls through late. Given how thin the pool of tradeable industrial buildings can run in Edenvale and along Monterey Road in a given quarter, some owners identify a DST interest specifically as insurance against a primary deal collapsing. Because DST subscription documents can typically be executed faster than a full building purchase, it also works well as the last-minute fallback when day 170 arrives and a directly owned deal still hasn't closed.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Committing Exchange Funds
sections.html:
Not every DST offering fits every exchanger, and the diligence looks different from buying a building directly. Before funds move, we confirm:

  • The sponsor's track record across prior offerings, beyond the one currently being marketed
  • Debt structure and whether it's non-recourse to the individual investor
  • Minimum hold period and any early redemption restrictions
  • Fee structure across acquisition, asset management, and disposition
  • How the offering's asset class lines up with the investor's actual goals

A sponsor with a strong current offering but a thin or troubled history on prior funds is a different risk profile than one with a decade of consistent execution, and that history rarely shows up in the offering memorandum itself.

sections.heading: The Tradeoffs Nobody Skips Past
sections.html:
A DST interest trades control for passivity. Once funds are placed, the investor has no vote on leasing decisions, capital improvements, or sale timing, that authority sits entirely with the sponsor. For an owner who's spent decades making those calls on a San Jose property personally, that shift is the real decision, not the tax mechanics. We walk through this tradeoff directly rather than treating the DST as a default answer for anyone tired of management.

Some owners find the loss of control liberating after years of fielding tenant calls at odd hours; others find it uncomfortable within the first year and wish they'd kept a directly owned property alongside it. Either reaction is normal, and we'd rather an owner hear both possibilities up front than discover one of them after the subscription is signed.

sections.heading: Coordinating Between the Sponsor, the QI, and Your Advisor
sections.html: A DST placement involves more parties moving in parallel than a direct property purchase: the sponsor's subscription documents, the qualified intermediary's transfer instructions, and your tax advisor's sign-off on suitability all need to close on the same timeline as the rest of the exchange. We keep these three tracks synchronized so a slow subscription document doesn't jeopardize the 180-day deadline. Confirm suitability and structure with your own tax and legal advisors before signing any subscription agreement.

faqs.q: Can I place only part of my exchange proceeds into a DST?
faqs.a: Yes, a DST interest can be sized to whatever portion of the exchange proceeds makes sense, and it's often paired with a directly owned replacement property to diversify between active and passive holdings.

faqs.q: Is a DST interest considered like-kind property for exchange purposes?
faqs.a: Structured correctly under existing guidance, a DST interest is generally treated as real property for exchange purposes, but the specific offering's structure needs to be confirmed by your tax advisor before funds are committed, since not every fractional ownership vehicle qualifies the same way.

faqs.q: Can I get my money back early if I need liquidity?
faqs.a: Most DST offerings have limited or no early redemption options, and hold periods commonly run five to ten years. This illiquidity is one of the biggest tradeoffs against the appeal of passive ownership, which is why we spend real time on hold period expectations before an owner commits exchange funds to a specific offering.

faqs.q: Do DST sponsors vary much in quality?
faqs.a: Significantly. Track record, fee structure, and debt terms differ widely between sponsors, which is why we check sponsor history on prior offerings rather than evaluating a single deal in isolation.

faqs.q: Why do San Jose owner-operators specifically ask about this option?
faqs.a: Long-held industrial and flex buildings around Edenvale and the Monterey Road corridor tend to sit with owners who built and ran them personally for decades, and a DST is often the first realistic path to stepping back from that role without giving up the exchange.
